title: Safe CRUD Workflows and Data Modification
learningObjectives: Perform INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE operations safely.
Use primary-key and business predicates to target intended rows.
Check the effect of a data modification before continuing.
Use transactions for multi-statement business changes.
Prefer soft deletion where audit or recovery requirements demand it.

understand.concept: CRUD represents the core lifecycle of stored data: create, read, update and delete. Safe workflows target exact rows, validate inputs and verify the result.
understand.whyItMatters: An UPDATE or DELETE without a correct predicate can change far more records than intended.
understand.analogy: Editing a single contact card requires checking the person's identity before saving or removing it.
understand.analogyLimit: A WHERE clause reduces accidental changes but does not replace authorization, transaction handling, backups or application-level validation.

explain.narrative:
## Safe CRUD sequence
Identify the target row using a stable key, validate the requested values, execute the statement, inspect the affected-row count and read back the result when needed. Use explicit column lists for INSERT and SELECT.

## UPDATE and DELETE safeguards
Never run a destructive statement against production data without reviewing the predicate and expected row count. A transaction can provide a rollback path before COMMIT. For records that must remain auditable, use a status or deleted_at field rather than physically deleting the row.

## Authorization
A correct key does not prove the caller may modify the record. Enforce authorization in the trusted service layer and scope updates by tenant/owner when the data model requires it.

examples.title: Create an asset register
examples.code: CREATE TABLE prj24_assets (asset_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, asset_name TEXT NOT NULL, quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity >= 0), asset_state TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (asset_state IN ('active','retired')));
examples.explanation: Defines an asset table with required values and constraints. The CHECK rules reject negative quantity and unsupported states.

examples.title: Create three asset records
examples.explanation: Adds two active assets and one retired asset. The explicit column order makes the insert's intent clear.

examples.title: Read one asset by its primary key
examples.code: SELECT asset_id, asset_name, quantity, asset_state FROM prj24_assets WHERE asset_id = 2;
examples.explanation: Reads a single asset by its unique key. Avoid returning unnecessary fields when a screen only needs a small projection.

examples.title: Update quantity for the selected asset
examples.code: UPDATE prj24_assets SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE asset_id = 2 AND quantity >= 1; SELECT asset_id, quantity FROM prj24_assets WHERE asset_id = 2;
examples.explanation: Decrements quantity only when the asset exists and has at least one unit. Application code should verify exactly one row changed before reporting success.

examples.title: Retire an asset without deleting its history
examples.code: UPDATE prj24_assets SET asset_state = 'retired' WHERE asset_id = 1; SELECT asset_id, asset_name, asset_state FROM prj24_assets WHERE asset_id = 1;
examples.explanation: Uses a status change instead of physical deletion so the asset record remains available for audit and historical reports.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and identify the predicates that protect the UPDATE statements. Explain why retiring a record may be safer than deleting it.
practise.independentTask: Create a customer CRUD workflow with a soft-delete flag. Write an update that changes one customer only when the authenticated tenant matches and verify the affected-row count.
hints: Use explicit columns in INSERT and SELECT.
Target rows with stable keys and required scope predicates.
Check affected-row counts before reporting success.
Consider soft deletion when history must be retained.

questions.explanation: CRUD names the four basic data lifecycle operations.

questions.prompt: Why include a WHERE clause in UPDATE?
options: To restrict which rows are changed
questions.answer: To restrict which rows are changed
questions.explanation: Without a suitable predicate, an UPDATE can affect every row.

questions.prompt: What should application code check after a targeted UPDATE?
options: The number of columns in the table
questions.explanation: The row count helps detect missing or unexpected targets.

options: When audit or historical records must remain available
When every table must be empty
questions.answer: When audit or historical records must remain available
questions.explanation: A status flag can preserve historical context while hiding a record from active workflows.

questions.prompt: Does a primary key alone prove authorization?
options: No; the trusted application must still check permission
Yes, every key is an access token
Only if it is an integer
Only after an index is added
questions.answer: No; the trusted application must still check permission
questions.explanation: Identification of a row and permission to modify it are separate concerns.
